name: Toussaint Louverture
info: Toussaint Louverture was a Haitian general, born into slavery in French Saint-Domingue, who became the most prominent leader of the Haitian Revolution and governor-general for life before dying a prisoner in France in 1803.

facts.born: 20 May 1743; thought to have been born on the Bréda plantation of Haut-du-Cap, Saint-Domingue, into slavery, the eldest son of Hyppolite, an Allada man, and his second wife Pauline
facts.died: 7 April 1803, in prison at Fort-de-Joux in Doubs, France, aged 59; suggested causes include exhaustion, malnutrition, apoplexy, pneumonia and possibly tuberculosis
facts.role: Lieutenant to Georges Biassou in the slave revolt of 1791; general allied with Spain (1793–1794) and then with Republican France (from 1794); Lieutenant Governor (1796) and top-ranking officer of Saint-Domingue (1797); Governor-General for life (1801–1802)
facts.known: Leading the Haitian Revolution; the declaration of Camp Turel in 1793; treaties with Britain and the United States; taking Spanish Santo Domingo and abolishing slavery there in 1801; the constitution of 1801; restoring the plantations with forced, paid labour; his arrest and death at Fort-de-Joux

t: Born into slavery and freed in the 1770s, Toussaint Louverture joined the slave revolt of 1791 when he was nearly 50 and became its most prominent general.

He fought first for Spain and then for Republican France once it moved to abolish slavery, defeated his rivals, took control of the whole island and in 1801 issued a constitution naming him governor-general for life.
Arrested by Napoleon's expedition in 1802 despite an amnesty, he died in a French prison in 1803, months before his lieutenant Jean-Jacques Dessalines led Haiti to independence.
dyk: Until 1938 historians believed that Louverture had been a slave until the revolution began. A marriage certificate and baptismal record dated between 1776 and 1777 later showed that he was already a freeman, and he had himself rented a coffee plantation with its 13 slaves.
ev: Toussaint is born into slavery on 20 May, thought to be on the Bréda plantation of Haut-du-Cap in Saint-Domingue
He is manumitted at some time between 1772 and 1776 and takes the name Toussaint Bréda
He joins the leaders of the slave revolt in the north at Morne-Rouge on 14 August and becomes secretary and lieutenant to Georges Biassou
Allied with the Spanish, he issues his declaration of Camp Turel on 29 August, calling for liberty and equality to reign in Saint-Domingue
He leaves the Spanish and is fighting officially for the French by 18 May, after the French government had proclaimed the abolition of slavery
He signs treaties with the British officer Thomas Maitland for the withdrawal of British troops from Saint-Domingue
He takes the Spanish part of the island in January and promulgates a constitution on 7 July that makes him governor-general for life
He is arrested on 7 June, deported to France and imprisoned at Fort-de-Joux, where he dies on 7 April 1803

sections.early:
Toussaint Louverture was born into slavery on 20 May 1743 in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, and is thought to have been born on the Bréda plantation of Haut-du-Cap. He was the eldest son of Hyppolite, an Allada man from the slave coast of West Africa, and his second wife Pauline, of the Aja ethnic group. Louverture's son Isaac later named Hyppolite's father as Gaou Guinou, a son of the King of Allada, though there is little extant evidence for the claim. The boy spoke first the Fon language of the Allada slaves, then Creole French. Small and thin, he was nicknamed Fatras-Bâton, "sickly stick", and was trained to work with horses as a coachman, away from the labour and punishments of the cane fields.

Baptised by the Jesuits, he was a devout Catholic throughout his life and gained some education from his godfather, Pierre-Baptiste. Documents found in the later 20th century show that he was manumitted at some time between 1772 and 1776, when François Antoine Bayon de Libertat was overseer, and took the name Toussaint Bréda. As one of the free people of colour he tried to become a planter, renting a small coffee plantation with its 13 slaves; one of them is believed to have been Jean-Jacques Dessalines. He bought several slaves, which was also one of the few legal ways to free relatives, and freed his sister Marie-Jean and others. The plantation failed and his first marriage, to Cécile, broke down. In 1782 he married Suzanne Simone-Baptiste. By 1789 he was a salaried employee on the Bréda plantation, in charge of its livestock.
sections.rise:
On 14 August 1791 two hundred slave foremen, Creoles and freed slaves met in secret at a plantation in Morne-Rouge to plan a revolt. Toussaint, wary of a public role after the execution of Vincent Ogé and Jean-Baptiste Chavannes, nominated Georges Biassou as leader and later joined him as secretary and lieutenant. A few days later a Vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman marked the public start of the rebellion in the north. Toussaint first sent his family to safety in Santo Domingo and hid his old overseer Bayon de Libertat. Like many devout Catholic slaves and freedmen he then identified as a royalist.

Through 1792 he held the fortified post of La Tannerie and the line of posts called the Cordon de l'Ouest, training his men in guerrilla tactics and "the European style of war". Some time in 1792–1793 he adopted the surname Louverture, "opening", most commonly explained by his ability to create openings in battle. He allied with the Spanish, probably in early June 1793, and on 29 August 1793 issued his declaration of Camp Turel: "I want Liberty and Equality to reign in St. Domingue." His force took the port of Gonaïves in December 1793. After France proclaimed the abolition of slavery on 4 February 1794 he changed sides; a letter shows him fighting for the French by 18 May 1794. He joined his 4,000 men to those of General Étienne Laveaux, ended the Spanish threat and contained the British. In 1796 he rescued Laveaux from a coup by the mulatto commander Jean-Louis Villatte, and Laveaux proclaimed him Lieutenant Governor.
sections.deeds:
In 1797 Louverture was appointed Saint-Domingue's top-ranking officer. That summer he arranged the return to France of the commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax, and in October 1798 a second French representative, Gabriel Hédouville, sailed away. On 30 April 1798 he signed a treaty with the British officer Thomas Maitland for the withdrawal of British troops from western Saint-Domingue, followed in August by treaties for the evacuation of the rest and a secret treaty lifting the naval blockade. He made a similar agreement with the United States under John Adams, while rebuffing suggestions from both powers that he declare independence. In the War of the South, begun in June 1799, he defeated General André Rigaud, who fled in August 1800.

In January 1801, against Napoleon Bonaparte's orders, Louverture and his nephew Hyacinthe Moïse invaded Spanish Santo Domingo, abolished slavery there and so controlled the entire island. Believing that the freedom of its people depended on the colony's economic viability, he restored the plantation system with paid labour, using diplomacy and force to return field hands to the estates, and he allowed white planters who had fled to come back. The constitution he promulgated on 7 July 1801 made him governor-general for life with near absolute powers and the right to choose his successor. Its Article 1 acknowledged Saint-Domingue as a colony of France, and Article 3 declared: "There cannot exist slaves, servitude is therein forever abolished. All men are born, live and die free and French."
sections.opponents:
Louverture's motives were disputed in his own time and since. Sonthonax, expelled in 1797, accused him of royalist, counter-revolutionary and pro-independence tendencies. The historian Beaubrun Ardouin argued that he was indifferent to black freedom and changed sides in 1794 out of concern for his safety and resentment of the Spanish; C. L. R. James tied the change to the emancipation decree, and Thomas Ott sees him as "both a power-seeker and sincere abolitionist". Rigaud claimed that he was conspiring with the British to restore slavery. His desire for personal power, the expulsion of Sonthonax and his rehabilitation of the white planters have all attracted historical criticism.

His rule bore hard on those it had freed. Workers staged small rebellions against poor conditions, their lack of real freedom and their fear of a return to slavery; they wanted smallholdings of their own. The constitution of 1801 confirmed forced labour and the importation of workers through the slave trade. A rebellion against forced labour led by his nephew Moïse in October 1801 was violently repressed, which cost him support when the French arrived. In the War of the South his lieutenant Dessalines became infamous for massacring mulatto captives and civilians: the French general Pamphile de Lacroix suggested 10,000 deaths, C. L. R. James only a few hundred. As ruler he discouraged Vodou and eventually persecuted its followers. Seeking British support, he betrayed Isaac Sasportas, who had planned a slave rising in Jamaica and was hanged in Kingston on 23 December 1799.
sections.last:
Napoleon sent an expedition of 20,000 men under his brother-in-law, General Charles Emmanuel Leclerc, to restore French authority and possibly slavery as well, with secret orders to deport all black officers. Louverture planned to burn the coastal cities, retreat into the mountains and wait for yellow fever to weaken the French. In late January 1802 Henri Christophe burned Cap-Français, but communications failed: Paul Louverture was tricked into letting the French occupy Santo Domingo. Months of inconclusive fighting ended when Christophe and then Dessalines went over to the French. On 6 May 1802 Louverture rode into Cap-Français and acknowledged Leclerc's authority in return for an amnesty for himself and his remaining generals. He was placed under house arrest on his property at Ennery.

On 22 May Dessalines denounced Louverture's conduct to Leclerc, and several authors, including Louverture's son Isaac, hold him at least partly responsible for the arrest. General Jean-Baptiste Brunet invited Louverture to a meeting; accounts differ on the pretext. On 7 June 1802 Louverture and a hundred members of his circle were seized and deported. Boarding the frigate Créole, he said that the French had cut down "only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again from the roots, for they are numerous and they are deep." On 25 August he was imprisoned at Fort-de-Joux in Doubs, where he wrote a memoir. His guards and the medical staff refused him proper care, one guard admitting that he did so because Louverture was black. He died in prison on 7 April 1803, aged 59.
sections.legacy:
Louverture died before the final and most violent stage of the Haitian Revolution, but his achievements set the grounds for the Haitian army's victory. Dessalines led the forces that defeated a French army ravaged by yellow fever; the last major battle was fought at Vertières on 18 November 1803, and independence was declared on 1 January 1804 under the name Haiti, after the indigenous Taíno name "Ayiti". Haiti was the first independent black republic in the Americas and the second independent nation in the Western Hemisphere. France recognised it in 1825, only after forcing it to agree to an indemnity of 150 million gold francs, and the United States under Abraham Lincoln in 1862. With Dessalines, Louverture is known as one of the "Fathers of Haiti".

During the 19th century African Americans referred to Louverture as an example of how to reach freedom, and John Brown claimed his influence in planning the raid on Harpers Ferry. On 29 August 1954 the Haitian ambassador to France inaugurated a stone cross in his memory at the foot of Fort de Joux, and the French government later presented soil from the fort to Haiti as a symbolic transfer of his remains. The Duvalier dictatorship used him as a national hero to promote Haitian identity and to justify its own rule. An inscription in his memory was placed on the wall of the Panthéon in Paris in 1998. His biographer Sudhir Hazareesingh describes him as "the epitome of the charismatic military leader", sober, sleeping only a few hours a night and of great physical endurance.

summary: Toussaint Louverture, born into slavery in Saint-Domingue in 1743 and freed in the 1770s, became the leading general of the Haitian Revolution. He drove out Spanish and British forces, ruled the whole island under his constitution of 1801 and restored its plantations with forced labour. Seized by the French in 1802, he died in prison in 1803.
references: Madison Smartt Bell, Toussaint L'Ouverture: A Biography (Vintage Books, 2008)
Charles Forsdick, Toussaint Louverture: A Black Jacobin in the Age of Revolutions (Pluto Press, 2017)
Robin Blackburn, The Overthrow of Colonial Slavery 1776–1848 (Verso Books, 2011)
notes: The article gives the birth date 20 May 1743 in the lead without hedging, but says only that he 'is thought to have been born on the Bréda plantation'. Its ages do not all agree with 1743: 'nearly 50' at the start of the revolution (lead), 'nearly 48' at 'the start of the revolution' (second marriage section), 59 at death. I kept 1743, circa false, and used 'nearly 50' once.

First marriage: the article says he met and married Cécile 'between 1761 and 1777' and that his eldest child Toussaint Jr. died in 1785 aged 24, which sits oddly with manumission in 1772-1776 and a 'formal Catholic wedding once freed'. I gave no date for the first marriage.
The article spells the son both 'Issac' and 'Isaac'; I used Isaac.
Change of sides in 1794: the article gives 4 May (Ardouin), 6 May (Ott), June (James) and a letter proving 18 May at the latest. I used the 18 May letter.

Villatte's coup: the article says '20 March' after a sentence on 1796, and that Louverture 'was promoted to commander of the West Province two months later, and in 1797 was appointed as Saint-Domingue's top-ranking officer'; the Lieutenant Governor proclamation is undated in the article; I placed it in 1796 with the rescue, as the sequence implies. Editor may prefer to drop '(1796)' in the role fact.
Article 3 as quoted in the article has an editorial '[in Saint-Domingue]'; I left the bracket out of the quotation.
The article says the constitution acknowledged Saint-Domingue as 'a single colony of the French Empire'; I wrote 'a colony of France'.
'against Napoleon Bonaparte's orders': the article says Napoleon forbade him to invade Spanish Santo Domingo and that he coerced Roume into giving permission.
'Governor-General for life (1801-1802)': the end year is mine, from his capitulation and arrest in 1802.
'His biographer Sudhir Hazareesingh': the article calls him 'historian and author' and 'author of Black Spartacus'; 'biographer' is my word - change to 'The historian' if preferred.
The dyk's '13 slaves' plantation was rented 'from his future son-in-law' (not named in the article).

Left out: the Freemasonry suggestion, his children and their later lives, the Third Commission's sending of his sons to France as schooling and as hostages, the 'soul of a white man' exchange with Sonthonax.

Left out for length (all in the article): his father's enslavement by Dahomey and sale to the slave ship Hermione, the 1791 negotiations with Governor Blanchelande, Article 6 on Catholicism (the persecution of Vodou is in the opponents section), his thirty-one properties and income of almost 300,000 colonial livres.
